title: Vision Without Execution is Hallucination
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Taking an Edison line he gave his students as birthday words of wisdom, Stuart argues that vision is cheap and execution is where the work and the credibility live. The framing claim is pedagogical: teachers should represent success to their students, and life instruction rings hollow unless it is rooted in demonstrable effort in the teacher's own life, so modelling applies to teaching success just as it applies to academic content. He then exposes his own vision-execution gaps in two areas, a rightly ordered life and writing for impact, admitting in each case to the unglamorous and often failed daily actions the vision actually requires. The writing section is the sharpest, describing execution as solitary hours, doubt and midnight calls to web hosting support rather than anything exciting. He then reports a classroom routine in which he asks students how many know an adult who dislikes a significant chunk of their life, and typically eighty to ninety percent raise their hands. The follow-up question, whether any of those adults sat in ninth grade hoping to end up that way, is the pivot to his point that nobody aspires to a frustrating life. Stuart closes by arguing that students' aspirations, realistic or not, deserve time spent thinking about how vision becomes execution.
points: Stuart's credibility test for teachers is concrete: do not give students life instruction that is not backed by demonstrable effort in your own life, because modelling works for teaching success as it does for teaching content.

He makes the vision-execution gap legible by pairing each aspiration with its unglamorous daily cost, including saying no to good ideas and not bringing essays home, and he admits he broke that one twice last week.
The account of writing for impact reframes creative work as consistency plus refusal of distraction, down to midnight calls to hosting support, rather than as inspiration.

His classroom hand-raise routine, where eighty to ninety percent of students know an adult who dislikes a big part of their life, is a cheap and reusable way to make the stakes of goal-setting vivid to teenagers.
The closing claim is that even unrealistic student aspirations deserve class time spent converting them into execution, which is a defence of spending scarce minutes on character work.
quotes: The vision part tends to be easy, for both my students and me. The execution part is harder; it's also where the magic happens.

We want to represent success to our students, as my friend Luke Wilcox from East Kentwood puts it. How hollow would it be if I shared words of wisdom (or any kind of life instruction) that wasn't rooted in demonstrable effort in my own life? Modeling works for many kinds of academic instruction; it also works in those moments when we're trying to teach success.
See what I mean about the vision part being easy? Many folks want a rightly ordered life. But the execution part — actually doing the things that lead to the vision — that's hard.

But executing on such visions is — I promise — not at all exciting . It's sitting by yourself with a computer, pulling your hair, trying to figure out how to say what you mean, trying to silence the doubting voices.
The answer, of course, is none. Nobody, as a ninth grader, aspires to live a frustrating life.

They envision dirt bikes or white doctors' coats or book signings or exotic travel — and if not things this specific then feelings like peace, contentment, excitement, engagement, creativity. And while some of their aspirations may not be realistic, all of them deserve some time to think through what it might mean to turn vision into execution in their own lives.
